passages.original: qui ex duobus legitimis alterum in adoptionem dederat, alterum abdicaverat, sustulit nothum; institute herede abdicato decessit. tres omnes de bonis contendunt. nothum , qui non sit legitimus, Graeci vocant; Latinum rei nomen, ut Cato quoque in oratione quadam testatus est, non habemus ideoque utimur peregrino. sed ad propositum.
passages.english: A man who had two legitimate sons, of whom he had given one in adoption and disowned the other, acknowledged a bastard son; having appointed the disowned son as heir, he died. All three contend over the estate. The Greeks call one who is not legitimate *nothos* [bastard]; we have no Latin name for the thing, as Cato too attested in one of his speeches, and so we use the foreign word. But to return to the subject.
passages.notes: 'sustulit' (literally 'raised up') refers to formally acknowledging and rearing a child. The Greek term appears in the text in the Latin accusative form 'nothum'.
